books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Daniel Webster, speech in the Senate, March 7, 1850

stimulus.source_note: Daniel Webster, speech in the Senate, March 7, 1850 (Congressional Globe, 31st Congress, 1st session, Appendix — Webster's revised text). Public domain.
stimulus.text:
Mr. President, — I wish to speak to-day, not as a Massachusetts man, nor as a Northern man, but as an American, and a member of the Senate of the United States.

. . .

I speak to-day for the preservation of the Union. “Hear me for my cause.” I speak to-day, out of a solicitous and anxious heart, for the restoration to the country of that quiet and that harmony which make the blessings of this Union so rich and so dear to us all.

. . .

Desirous of immediate connection with the United States, [California's] Senators were appointed and representatives chosen, . . . asking, in behalf of their State, that the state may be admitted into this Union as one of the United States. This constitution, Sir, contains an express prohibition against slavery, or involuntary servitude, in the State of California. . . . This prohibition against slavery, it is said, was inserted with entire unanimity.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Webster's speech is best understood as an effort to persuade the Senate that

options.text: the North should accept the spread of slavery to preserve the peace.
options.misconception: Webster's plea is for the Union, not for slavery's spread; the speech asks the Senate to settle the crisis, not to extend slavery.

options.text: keeping the Union together mattered more than winning the slavery argument in the territories.
California should be divided into free and slave halves along the Missouri Compromise line.
options.misconception: Background from the books: dividing California was proposed by others, but Webster's speech backs admitting California whole, under its own free-state constitution.

options.text: the South had no real grievances and should drop its threats of secession.
options.misconception: Webster treats the danger to the Union as real — he speaks out of “a solicitous and anxious heart” — rather than dismissing Southern anger.

rationales.A: Webster's plea is for the Union, not for slavery's spread; the speech asks the Senate to settle the crisis, not to extend slavery.
rationales.B: Webster says he speaks “for the preservation of the Union” and for “the restoration to the country of that quiet and that harmony” — Union first, sectional victory second.
rationales.C: Background from the books: dividing California was proposed by others, but Webster's speech backs admitting California whole, under its own free-state constitution.
rationales.D: Webster treats the danger to the Union as real — he speaks out of “a solicitous and anxious heart” — rather than dismissing Southern anger.
rationales.general:
1. Catch Webster's own order of values: first the Union, then quiet and harmony for the whole country.
2. Ask what he is willing to set aside: a sectional victory on slavery in the territories.
3. Weigh the speech's center of gravity: it is a plea for the Union to hold, not a brief for either side.
Remember: a speech that opens by renouncing sectional labels is asking its hearers to rank the Union above the argument.
